[exd5] exchanges it: after [exd5 cxd5 d4] the game is an Exchange Caro-Kann. The Two Knights [Nc3] defends it with a piece, the advance [e5] pushes it past the attack, and the Endgame Offer [d3] holds it with a pawn, inviting [d3 dxe4 dxe4 Qxd1+] with the queens off.
[Bd3] and [Qe2] defend e4 too, and are about equal: the bishop blocks the d-pawn, and the queen stands in front of the f1 bishop.

Everything else lets Black take on e4, with the f3 knight attacked once the pawn has gone: after [c3 dxe4] or [d4 dxe4] the knight has to move. That costs White between half a pawn and two pawns, from [h4] and [h3], which at least give the knight the h2 square, through [d4], [Ne5], [a4], [c3], [a3], [Nh4], [Be2], [g3], [Nd4], [Na3], [Rg1], [Ng1], [c4], [b3], [Ng5], [b4] and [g4]. [Ke2] gives up castling as well, and three bishop moves give the bishop away: [Bc4 dxc4], [Bb5 cxb5] and [Ba6 Nxa6].

This is a position where the shallow search is easily fooled. [c3] looks fine at depth 8, +0.19, as good as the real defences, but deeper it loses more than a pawn (-1.22 at depth 16, -1.16 at depth 25). [h4] goes the other way, from -1.27 at depth 8 to -0.53. [Nc3] is +0.52 at depth 8 and +0.28 deeper, while [d3] grows from +0.21 to +0.34.

The Advance Variation. White's pawn on e5 gains space and takes f6 from Black's knight, and the pawn chain d4-e5 points at Black's kingside. In return the chain shuts nothing in on Black's side: the light-squared bishop can still come out, and the chain can be attacked at its base with ...c5.

The two classical answers do exactly that. [Bf5] develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 closes its diagonal, and is the engine's best, +0.25 for White. The Botvinnik-Carls [c5] strikes at d4 at once, a little behind at +0.39. [e6] prepares ...c5 too, but shuts in the c8 bishop, which leaves White about half a pawn.

The rest are slower: [Bd7], the queen moves [Qc7], [Qb6] and [Qa5+], [a6], [g6], [Nh6], [h6], [a5], [h5], [f6], [Be6], [b6], [Na6], [Qd7], [b5] and [Nd7] cost between seven-tenths of a pawn and a pawn and a quarter. [f5], [Kd7] and [g5] weaken Black's king.
Four moves lose material. [Nf6] puts the knight where the e5 pawn takes it, [Nf6 exf6]; [Bg4] is taken by [Bg4 Qxg4] and [Bh3] by [Bh3 gxh3]; and [Qd6] gives the queen to [Qd6 exd6].

[Bf5] gains with depth (+0.58, +0.35, +0.25 for White at depths 8, 16 and 25), and [c5] less so (+0.51, +0.41, +0.39). The move that fools a shallow search is [Be6]: at depth 8 it looks like more than two pawns for White, at depth 16 and 25 it is a pawn at most, slow but not losing.

m.n: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Botvinnik-Carls Defense

a: The main line of the Caro-Kann. White's knight stands in the centre, and Black has three classical ways to go on, all about a third of a pawn behind and too close for the table to separate.

The Classical [Bf5] develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain with a hit on the knight, and after [Bf5 Ng3 Bg6] it settles on g6. The Karpov [Nd7] prepares ...Ngf6 so that a knight exchange on f6 can be met by a knight. [Nf6] challenges the e4 knight straight away: after [Nf6 Nxf6+] Black chooses between ...exf6 and ...gxf6, both leaving the pawns damaged.

A second group costs a little more, between half a pawn and nine-tenths: the fianchetto [g6], the Finnish [h6], [a6], the queen moves [Qd5], [Qc7], [Qb6] and [Qa5+], and [Na6], [Be6], [e6] and [Bd7]. [e6] in particular shuts in the c8 bishop, whose diagonal is open.

[h5], [Nh6], [b5], [b6], [Qd7] and the pawn breaks [c5] and [e5], which White can meet with [c5 dxc5] or [e5 dxe5], cost from one to one and two-thirds pawns. [f6], [f5] and [g5] loosen Black's king, and [Kd7] blocks Black's queen and bishop. The rest give material away: [Bg4] to [Bg4 Qxg4], [Bh3] to [Bh3 Nxh3], [Qd6] to [Qd6 Nxd6], and [Qxd4] the queen to [Qxd4 Qxd4].

Which of the three is best depends on the depth. At depth 8 the shallow search prefers [Nf6] by far, giving White only +0.11, ahead of [Nd7] (+0.54) and [Bf5] (+0.57). At depth 16 [Bf5] leads at +0.26 and [Nd7] trails at +0.63; at depth 25 [Nd7] is the engine's best at +0.32, [Bf5] +0.36 and [Nf6] +0.42. None of the three is a mistake.

Black's pawn stands on e4, and White is a pawn down. [Nxe4] takes it at once and is the only move that keeps White's edge, +0.43: the knight comes to the centre, and the main lines go on with [Nxe4 Bf5], [Nxe4 Nd7] or [Nxe4 Nf6].

[Nge2] is the only other move that keeps the balance, aiming to take on e4 with a knight a move later, from g3 or c3. The gambits are a step down: the von Hennig [Bc4] develops first and leaves the pawn, and the Rasa-Studier [f3] offers a second pawn after [f3 exf3], both about half a pawn for Black.

Everything else simply leaves White a pawn down: [h3], [a3], [Qd2], [Bg5], [g4], [a4], [Be3], [Bf4], [h4], [g3], [Be2], [Qe2], [Nce2], [Rb1], [Nh3], [Bd2], [Qh5], [b3], [Nb1], [b4] and [Na4], between four-tenths and a pawn and a half. [d5] gives a second pawn to [d5 cxd5], [Ke2] and [Kd2] put the king in the way, and [f4] allows [f4 exf3], taking en passant and opening White's king.

Many moves give a piece away. [Nf3] and [Bd3] land on squares the e4 pawn attacks, as in [Nf3 exf3] and [Bd3 exd3]; [Bb5] and [Nb5] are taken by the c6 pawn, [Bb5 cxb5]; [Bh6] by [Bh6 Nxh6], [Ba6] by [Ba6 Nxa6], and [Nd5] by [Nd5 cxd5]. The queen moves [Qf3], [Qd3] and [Qg4] give the queen itself, the last to [Qg4 Bxg4].

[Nxe4] grows with depth: +0.28 at depth 8, +0.24 at depth 16, +0.43 at depth 25. [Nge2] looks a third of a pawn worse than equal at depth 8 (-0.33) and is about equal deeper; [h3] starts at a full pawn for Black and settles at four-tenths.

The Botvinnik-Carls Defence of the Advance Variation. Black's pawn on c5 strikes at d4, the base of White's pawn chain, and none of Black's pieces is developed yet. White has 38 moves, and four of them keep a quarter to two-fifths of a pawn.

[Nf3] is the engine's best, +0.40: it defends d4 with a piece and develops. Taking with [dxc5] is almost as good, +0.36: White wins the pawn and gives up the base of the pawn chain. [c4] strikes at d5 in return, and [c3] supports d4 with a pawn, both about a quarter of a pawn.

[Bb5+], [Nc3], [f4], [Nd2], [Ne2], [Bf4], [Na3], [h3] and [Bd3] are close to equal, and [Be3] a little worse. Slow moves such as [a3], [a4], [b3], [h4], [Qd3], [Be2], [Qh5], [b4], [g3], [Bd2], [f3], [Qd2], [Bg5] and [Qf3] give Black a fifth of a pawn to six-tenths.

[e6] gives a pawn to [e6 Bxe6], [Qe2] blocks the f1 bishop, [g4] and [Nh3] loosen the kingside, and [Ke2] and [Kd2] give up castling. Four moves give material away: [Bc4] to [Bc4 dxc4], [Ba6] to [Ba6 Nxa6], [Bh6] to [Bh6 Nxh6], and the queen to [Qg4 Bxg4].

Two of the most natural moves are overrated by a shallow search. At depth 8 [dxc5] looks like a pawn for White (+0.96) and [c3] almost as much (+0.77); at depth 25 they are +0.36 and +0.21. [Nf3] is steadier, +0.52, +0.50 and +0.40 at depths 8, 16 and 25, and ends up the best. [h3] is the oddest: -0.13 at depth 8, the best of all at depth 16 (+0.34), and equal at depth 25.

A symmetrical pawn structure: one centre pawn each on d4 and d5, and open e- and c-files. Nothing is under attack, and Black has a wide choice of developing moves that keep White's edge to a fifth of a pawn or less.

[Bf5], [Nc6] and [Nf6] are the engine's best, +0.12 to +0.20 for White, too close to separate. [Bf5] develops the light-squared bishop before ...e6 shuts it in, [Nc6] puts pressure on d4, and [Nf6] covers e4 and prepares to castle. [Bg4] pins the f3 knight, a little behind at +0.34.

Quieter moves cost a little more: [a6], [e6], [h6], [Be6], [g6] and [Bd7] are between a third and half a pawn. The early queen moves [Qd6], [Qc7], [Qa5+] and [Qb6], and [Nd7], which blocks the c8 bishop, give White most of a pawn. [h5], [b6], [a5], [Nh6], [f6], [Qd7] and [Na6] do little.

Some moves weaken Black seriously. The break [e5] gives a pawn to [e5 dxe5], [b5] and [g5] loosen the position, and [f5] weakens e5 and Black's king. [Kd7] puts the king in front of its pieces, more than three and a half pawns, and [Bh3] gives the bishop away to [Bh3 gxh3].

The shallow search ranks the moves differently. At depth 8 [Nc6] is the best (+0.12) and [Bf5] looks like half a pawn for White (+0.52); at depth 25 [Bf5] is the engine's best (+0.12). [Nd7] goes the other way: +0.39 at depth 8, +0.80 at depth 25, so blocking the bishop costs more than it seems.

The Exchange Variation. The pawn structure is symmetrical, one centre pawn each on d4 and d5, with the e-file open for White and the c-file for Black. Nothing is attacked, and White's edge is small whatever White plays: the best moves keep about a quarter of a pawn.

[c3] and the Panov [c4] are the engine's best, +0.29 and +0.27. [c3] supports d4 with a pawn and keeps the structure, the classical way to play the Exchange; [c4] attacks d5 at once and leads to open positions, often with an isolated pawn. [Bd3] and [Nf3] develop first, +0.17 and +0.13, and [Bd3] keeps an eye on h7.

A long list of moves is about equal: [Be3], [h3], [Ne2], [Bf4], [Nc3], [Bg5], [Be2], [Bb5+], [Qd3], [a4] and [Nd2]. Then come slower moves, [a3], [h4], [Na3], [g3], [Bd2], and early queen moves such as [Qd2], [Qf3], [Qe2] and [Qh5], between a tenth of a pawn and half a pawn for Black.

[b3], [f3], [b4] and [f4] loosen White's position, the Bulla Attack [g4] gives a pawn to [g4 Bxg4], [Nh3] goes to the rim, and [Kd2] and [Ke2] give up castling, about a pawn. Four moves give material away: [Bc4] to [Bc4 dxc4], [Ba6] to [Ba6 Nxa6], [Bh6] to [Bh6 Nxh6], and the queen to [Qg4 Bxg4].

The order of the best moves depends on the depth. At depth 8 [c4] leads (+0.39) and [c3] is only sixth (+0.15); at depth 16 [c3] falls to +0.09, well behind [c4], [Nf3] and [Bd3], and at depth 25 it is the best at +0.29. [Qd3] looks like half a pawn for Black at depth 8 and is equal at depth 25.

m.n: Caro-Kann Defense: Exchange Variation, Bulla Attack

a: White has no centre pawn and Black has one on d5. Nothing is attacked, and the position is close to equal whatever White plays: the best moves keep less than a fifth of a pawn.

[d4] is the natural move, staking a claim in the centre and reaching the Exchange Variation's structure, with one pawn each on d4 and d5. [Ne5], the Apocalypse Attack, jumps into the centre at once, and [c3] prepares d4 with a pawn behind it. [Be2], [Nc3], [h3] and [Bb5+] are about equal too, the check being met by ...Nc6 or ...Bd7.

Slower moves cost a little: [b3], [a3], [a4], [d3], [g3], [c4], [Na3], [Bd3] and [Qe2], between a tenth of a pawn and a third. [Nd4], [h4], [b4], [Ng1], [Ng5] and [Rg1] give Black about half a pawn, and [Nh4] more than a pawn.
[Ke2] gives up castling, and [g4] drops a pawn to [g4 Bxg4]. Two bishop moves give the bishop away: [Bc4] to [Bc4 dxc4] and [Ba6] to [Ba6 Nxa6].

The scores are small, but the shallow search ranks them differently. At depth 8 [d4] (+0.15) and [a3] (+0.17) lead, while [c3] looks a little worse than equal (-0.17) and [Ne5] about equal; at depth 16 [c3] is best (+0.26), and at depth 25 [Ne5], [c3] and [d4] share the top at +0.15 to +0.18. [d4] is the steady choice, +0.15 to +0.20 at every depth.

The Queen's Gambit. The c4 pawn attacks d5, and Black has to decide what to do about the centre. Three answers stand out, and the engine cannot separate them: each leaves White the usual edge of about a third of a pawn. The Queen's Gambit Declined [e6] holds d5 with a pawn and keeps a rock-solid centre, but it shuts in the c8 bishop for a while. The Slav [c6] holds d5 just as firmly while keeping that bishop's diagonal open. The Queen's Gambit Accepted [dxc4] takes the pawn and gives up the centre for a moment in exchange for free development; White wins the pawn back, for instance with [dxc4 e3] followed by Bxc4, and trying to keep it with ...b5 backfires, as in [dxc4 e4 b5 a4].

Black can also hit back instead of defending. The Austrian [c5] strikes at d4 in return, but after [c5 cxd5 Qxd5 Nc3] Black's queen is chased around the board. The Chigorin [Nc6] develops pieces rather than defending with pawns, often pinning the f3 knight later with ...Bg4. The Albin Countergambit [e5] sacrifices a pawn for activity after [e5 dxe5 d4]. All three are playable but give White more than the main lines, around half a pawn to two-thirds.

Some developing moves forget to look after d5. The Marshall [Nf6] lets White take the centre with tempo: [Nf6 cxd5 Nxd5 e4]. The Baltic [Bf5] develops the bishop before ...e6, but leaves b7 undefended, which [Bf5 Qb3] attacks at once; the engine prefers [Bf5 cxd5]. [g6] prepares ...Bg7, but after [g6 cxd5 Qxd5 Nc3] the queen is again a target. These cost Black between two-thirds of a pawn and a pawn.

The weaker moves all give White a free hand in the centre, at more than a pawn. Queen moves such as [Qd6] and [Qd7] block Black's own bishops, and [Nd7] and [Bd7] do the same. [Be6] stands in front of the e-pawn. [Bg4] takes the bishop away from the queenside while d5 still needs support, and the engine's answer is again [Bg4 cxd5], worth almost two pawns to White. Flank moves such as [a6], [h6], [a5], [h5] and [b6] do nothing for d5, [f5] and [f6] loosen Black's king, and [Na6] and [Nh6] put a knight on the rim.

A few moves simply lose material or time. The Zilbermints Gambit [b5] gives a pawn away to [b5 cxb5], and [g5] drops one to [g5 Bxg5]. [Kd7] blocks the queen and the light-squared bishop with the king itself, at more than three pawns. Worst of all, [Bh3] gives the bishop away to [Bh3 gxh3].

The three main defences hold up at depth: at depth 25 [e6], [c6] and [dxc4] are -0.29, -0.32 and -0.34 from Black's side. The shallow search underrates the Slav [c6], -0.56 at depth 8, while [e6] and [dxc4] are already around -0.30 there. The Albin [e5] does best at depth 16, -0.48, and slips back to -0.69 at depth 25. The move that fools a shallow search most is [Bd7]: at depth 8 it looks about as good as the Marshall [Nf6] (-0.79), but it costs a pawn and two-thirds at depth 25. [Nh6] is similar, -1.07 at depth 8 and almost two pawns deeper.

t: Queen's Gambit Accepted. Black grabs the pawn, giving up the centre for a moment in exchange for free development.
Queen's Gambit Declined. Black supports d5 with a pawn and keeps a firm foothold in the centre. The price: the c8 bishop is temporarily locked in.
Black supports d5 with the c-pawn and keeps the c8–h3 diagonal open, solving the QGD's main problem.
Black answers a gambit with a gambit, sacrificing the e-pawn for quick activity. Objectively a bit dubious, but White needs to know what to do.

a: White has 27 moves here, and two of them keep White's full opening edge. The Queen's Gambit [c4] attacks d5 at once and asks Black to decide about the centre: take with [c4 dxc4], hold with [c4 e6] or [c4 c6], or counter-attack with [c4 e5]. [Nf3], the Zukertort, is almost as good and more flexible: it develops, keeps an eye on e5, and can still turn into a Queen's Gambit with c4 a move later.

Many players prefer a system they can set up against anything. The London [Bf4] brings the dark-squared bishop out before e3 shuts it in. [e3] prepares the Colle or the Stonewall, with Bd3, Nd2 and sometimes f4. [c3] supports d4 and keeps the queen's diagonal to b3 open, and [g3] prepares a fianchetto in the style of the Catalan. These moves keep the balance rather than fight for an advantage: the engine rates them all between equal and +0.2.

Sharper players look for an early fight. [Nc3] develops but blocks the c-pawn; after [Nc3 Nf6 Bg5] it becomes the Veresov. The Levitsky [Bg5] develops the bishop with a hit on e7 straight away. Both are about equal. The Blackmar-Diemer Gambit [e4] goes further and gives up a pawn for quick development: after [e4 dxe4 Nc3 Nf6 f3], White hopes to open the f-file against Black's king, but the engine prefers Black by more than half a pawn. The Mason [f4] grabs e5 but weakens e4 and the diagonal to White's king.

The rest give Black the easier game. Early queen moves such as [Qd3] (the Amazon Attack) and [Qd2] get in the way of White's own bishops. [Bd2] and [Be3] develop the bishop to passive squares, the last one in front of the e-pawn. Flank moves such as [a3], [h3], [b3], [a4], [h4] and [b4], and the knight moves to the rim [Na3] and [Nh3], do little for the centre.

A few moves are real mistakes. [f3] takes the best square from the g1 knight and weakens the king, and [Kd2] blocks the bishop and the queen with the king itself. The Zurich Gambit [g4] simply drops a pawn to [g4 Bxg4]. Worst of all, [Bh6] gives a whole bishop away to [Bh6 gxh6].

The Queen's Gambit is a move the engine appreciates more the deeper it looks: [c4] is only +0.15 at depth 8, +0.32 at depth 16 and +0.38 at depth 25. [e3] goes the other way, the shallow search's favourite at +0.44 and only +0.15 at depth 25, and the London [Bf4] ends at +0.06 after +0.15 and +0.22. The Blackmar-Diemer Gambit [e4] looks like a pawn lost at depth 8 (-0.98) and costs about half a pawn deeper (-0.51), while [h4] looks harmless at depth 8 (-0.11) and costs half a pawn at depth 25 (-0.48).

t: The Queen's Gambit, known since the 15th century. White offers the c-pawn to pull Black's d-pawn away from the centre so White can play e4. It is not a real gambit: the pawn can almost always be regained.
Black develops and keeps an eye on e4.

a: Black is a pawn up, with a pawn on c4, and the question is how White wins it back. The pawn on c4 is hard to keep for long: once the e-pawn moves, the f1 bishop attacks it. The engine's favourite is the Central Variation [e4] (Saduleto in the lichess list), which takes the whole centre and opens the bishop's diagonal in one go. Black has to react at once, usually by striking back with [e4 e5]. Trying to keep the pawn with [e4 b5] runs into [e4 b5 a4], as the lines below show.

The Normal Variation [Nf3] and the Old Variation [e3] are calmer and almost as good. [Nf3] develops first and stops ...e5; the classical main line continues [Nf3 Nf6 e3 e6 Bxc4]. [e3] opens the bishop at once, and Black's most direct answer is [e3 e5].

[Nc3] and the Mannheim [Qa4+] only keep the balance. The knight on c3 does not attack c4, so Black can answer [Nc3 a6] and prepare ...b5 to hold the pawn. [Qa4+] wins the pawn back quickly with Qxc4, but brings the queen out very early.

Moves that do nothing about c4 leave Black a healthy extra pawn, at around half a pawn to a pawn for Black: bishop moves such as [Bf4], [Bg5], [Bd2] and [Be3], the slow [g3], [a3], [h3], [h4], [a4] and [f4], or [Nd2], [Qd2] and [Qc2]. [f3] prepares e4 but takes the best square from the g1 knight, [Na3] puts a knight on the rim, and [d5] pushes past without winning the pawn back.

Watch the c4 pawn: it attacks b3 and d3. So [b3] only gives it a target to take, [b3 cxb3], and [b4] allows it to capture en passant, [b4 cxb3], leaving Black two pawns up. Worst of all, [Qb3] and [Qd3] put the queen where that pawn takes it: [Qd3 cxd3]. Other mistakes are [g4], which drops a pawn to [g4 Bxg4], [Nh3], [Kd2], and [Bh6], which gives a bishop away to [Bh6 gxh6].

t: White builds an ideal pawn centre straight away and plans to win back c4 later.
A flexible developing move that also prevents ...e5, Black's most natural central break.

a: White has built the ideal centre and is ready to win back c4 with Bxc4. The score table has no depth-25 scores for this position, so the scores here were computed on the spot: at depth 20 for the six main replies, at depth 16 for the rest.

Two replies share first place and keep White's edge to under half a pawn. The Alekhine System [Nf6] attacks e4 at once; White usually gains space with [Nf6 e5 Nd5], and the knight finds a good central square. The McDonnell Defence [e5] strikes back at the centre before White has finished developing, as in [e5 Nf3 exd4 Bxc4]. The Modern Defence [Nc6] is just behind, putting pressure on d4 straight away.

[e6] and the Rubinstein Defence [c5] are a little less precise: [e6] frees the f8 bishop and prepares ...c5, while [c5] hits d4 at once. Holding the pawn with the Greco Variation [b5] is close too, but only if Black knows what comes next. White's best answer is [b5 a4], hitting the base of the pawn chain, and from there [b5 a4 a6] walks into a trap, while [b5 a4 c6 axb5 cxb5 Nc3] keeps White pressing.

Slower moves give White a pawn's worth or more. [a6], [g6] and [c6] take time without challenging the centre, and [c6] also takes the c6 square from Black's own knight. [Nd7], [Bd7] and [Be6] develop to passive squares; the bishop on e6 can be chased by [Be6 d5]. Queen moves such as [Qd6] and [Qd7] invite White's pieces to gain time, flank moves such as [a5], [b6], [h6] and [h5] do nothing for the centre, and [Na6] and [Nh6] put a knight on the rim. The Schwartz Defence [f5] and [f6] loosen Black's king, and [c3] simply gives the pawn back: [c3 bxc3].

The rest lose material. [g5] drops a pawn to [g5 Bxg5] and [Kd7] blocks Black's own pieces with the king. [Bg4] hangs the bishop to [Bg4 Qxg4], [Bf5] to [Bf5 exf5], and [Bh3] to [Bh3 gxh3]. Worst of all, the queen cannot join the fight yet: [Qxd4] grabs a pawn but loses the queen to [Qxd4 Qxd4], and [Qd5] loses it to [Qd5 exd5].

t: Black tries to keep the extra pawn by protecting c4. Greedy and risky: it weakens the queenside.
The most direct reply: Black hits back at the centre before White has finished developing.
Black defends d5 a second time while developing.
Develops and adds pressure on d5.
The point: this pawn cramps White, taking away c3 and e3 from White's pieces.

a: The Albin Countergambit. Black offers the e-pawn to open lines and, after it is taken, to drive the d-pawn to d4, where it cramps White's position. White has 31 moves, and one of them is clearly best.

Accepting with [dxe5] is the engine's choice by half a pawn, +0.79: White wins a pawn and Black has to prove the activity is worth it. At depth 14 Black's best replies, [dxe5 Ne7], [dxe5 dxc4] and the classical [dxe5 d4], are all about two-thirds of a pawn to a pawn behind.

Declining keeps less. [Nc3] develops and adds pressure on d5, +0.29, and [cxd5] takes the other pawn, +0.21. [e3] gives up most of the edge, and [Nf3] runs into [Nf3 e4], which chases the knight. [a3], [h3], [Qa4+], [Qd2], [g3], [h4], [Be3], [e4], [a4], [Bd2], [Na3], [Nd2], [Qb3], [Nh3], [Qc2] and [f3] all leave Black the better game, between a third of a pawn and a pawn and a quarter.

Some moves weaken White badly: [b3], [g4], [Qd3], which runs into [Qd3 dxc4], [c5], [f4], which gives a pawn to [f4 exf4], and [b4], which gives one to [b4 Bxb4+]. Three bishop moves lose the bishop: [Bg5] to [Bg5 Qxg5], [Bf4] to [Bf4 exf4] and [Bh6] to [Bh6 Nxh6]. Worst of all is [Kd2], putting the king in front of its own pieces in the open centre.

[dxe5] is the best move at every depth, +0.79 to +0.88 for White, and [Nc3] and [cxd5] stay well behind it. The move whose score depends most on depth is [Kd2]: three pawns for Black at depth 8, four at depth 16, more than five at depth 25. [b4] also gets worse the deeper one looks, from -1.83 to -2.63.

[h6], [Be7], [Nc6], the Small Center [d6], [b6] and [c6] keep the position closed for the moment, between two-thirds of a pawn and nine-tenths.

The rest let White build freely: [Ne7], [a5], [Bb4+], [h5], [Na6], the Mediterranean [Nf6], which is chased by [Nf6 e5], [g6], the queen moves [Qe7], [Qf6] and [Qh4], [Nh6], [Bd6], which blocks the d-pawn, and [f6]. Three moves give material away: [Bc5] to [Bc5 dxc5], [Ba3] to [Ba3 Nxa3], and the queen to [Qg5 Bxg5].

The French Defence. Black's pawn on e6 prepares ...d5, which will challenge e4 with a pawn the e6 pawn supports. The cost is that the c8 bishop's diagonal is shut for the time being.

[d4] is clearly White's best, +0.43: it takes the whole centre while it is free, and after [d4 d5] the main French begins, with White choosing between defending, advancing or exchanging the e4 pawn. [Nc3] and [Nf3] develop first and are a little behind, +0.25 and +0.20; after [Nc3 d5] White can still play d4.

Many moves keep about equality without fighting for the centre: [h3], the Réti-Spielmann [g3], [Be2], the Steiner [c4], the King's Indian Attack [d3], [c3], the Chigorin [Qe2], [Bd3], [a3], the Bird Invitation [Bb5], the La Bourdonnais [f4] and the Steinitz [e5], which advances before d4 can support the pawn.

The rest give Black a little: [a4], [h4], [Ne2], [Nh3], [Qf3], the Horwitz [b3], [Bc4], which runs into ...d5, [f3], [Na3], and the queen moves [Qg4] and [Qh5], from a fifth of a pawn to a half. [g4], the Banzai-Leong Gambit [b4], which gives a pawn to [b4 Bxb4], and [Ke2] cost about a pawn, and [Ba6] gives the bishop away to [Ba6 Nxa6].

[d4] is White's best at every depth, +0.44 at depth 8, +0.52 at depth 16 and +0.43 at depth 25. [Be2] is the move a shallow search overrates: at depth 8 it looks as good as [d4] (+0.46), but deeper it is only equal. [Nf3] goes the other way, from -0.05 at depth 8 to +0.20, and the Steiner [c4] from -0.36 to equality.

The Vienna Game. White's knight covers d5 and e4 and leaves the f-pawn free, so f4 is often White's next idea. It does not attack e5, and Black has two replies that leave White practically nothing, the engine giving White +0.04 and +0.12.

[Nc6] develops and defends e5, ready to meet [Nc6 f4] with ...exf4, or the Bishop's Opening set-up [Nc6 Bc4] with ...Nf6. [Nf6] counter-attacks e4 instead. White can then play the Vienna Gambit [Nf6 f4], take aim at f7 with [Nf6 Bc4], or keep it quiet with [Nf6 Nf3].

The bishop moves are a little less accurate. The Anderssen [Bc5] aims at f2 and stops d4 for the moment, and [Bb4] pins nothing yet but prepares to take on c3; both give White about a third of a pawn. [d6] is solid but passive, [Be7] and [Bd6] develop to modest squares, the second blocking the d-pawn, and [c6] prepares ...d5 slowly: all between half a pawn and two-thirds.

Slow pawn moves such as [a6], [h6], [c5] and [a5], the knight move [Ne7] and early queen moves such as [Qe7] and [Qf6] cost more. [d5] opens the centre too early, as after [d5 exd5] White's knight is already pointing at d5, and [b6], [h5], [g6] and [Nh6] do little. [f6] takes the knight's square and loosens Black's king, and [f5] gives a pawn to [f5 exf5].

The early queen raids lose time: [Qh4] is met by [Qh4 Nf3], and [Qg5] by [Qg5 d4], which develops a piece and hits e5 while attacking the queen; both are about two pawns for White. [Na6] puts the knight on the rim, [b5] drops a pawn to [b5 Nxb5], [g5] loosens the kingside, [Ke7] gives up castling, and [Ba3] gives a bishop away to [Ba3 bxa3].

Depth changes the order of the best moves. At depth 8 the shallow search prefers [Bc5] and [Nc6], both around +0.23 for White, and rates [Nf6] at +0.52. By depth 16 [Nf6] is already +0.13, and depth 25 confirms it at +0.12 while [Bc5] slips to +0.37: the counter-attack on e4 needs depth to be appreciated. [Be7] and [c6] are the opposite of tricky: they look like more than a pawn for White at depth 8 and only about half a pawn deeper.
White's knight attacks the e5 pawn, which nothing defends yet. Black has 29 moves, and the question is how to deal with that attack: defend the pawn, counterattack e4, or give it up.

The natural [Nc6] defends e5 and develops, leaving White about a fifth of a pawn. Petrov's Defence [Nf6] counterattacks e4 instead; the engine cannot tell it apart from [Nc6]. The Philidor [d6] defends with a pawn: solid, but it shuts in the f8 bishop, and White keeps more than half a pawn.

Other defences cost Black most of a pawn or more. The Gunderam [Qe7] and the McConnell [Qf6] defend with the queen, which then blocks a bishop or the g8 knight. [Bd6] defends but blocks the d-pawn. The Elephant Gambit [d5] and the Latvian Gambit [f5] hit back in the centre at the cost of a pawn, as in [d5 exd5].

Most other moves leave e5 hanging and cost more than a pawn: [Be7], [c6], [Ne7], [a6], [h6], [a5], [g6], and the bishop sorties [Bb4] and the Busch-Gass [Bc5], where White simply plays [Bc5 Nxe5]. The Damiano [f6] defends e5 but weakens Black's king: [f6 Nxe5] is strong anyway, because [f6 Nxe5 fxe5 Qh5 g6 Qxe5] gives check and forks the king and the h8 rook. [c5], [b6], [b5], [g5] and [Ke7] cost two pawns or more.
The three blunders put a piece where White takes it: [Ba3 Nxa3], [Qh4 Nxh4] and [Qg5 Nxg5].

Both sides have a pawn in the centre, and neither pawn can be taken yet. White has 29 moves, and the engine sees the position as close to equal whatever White chooses, with at most a fifth of a pawn to White.

The two best moves develop a knight. [Nf3] attacks e5 straight away and prepares to castle; the engine's reply is [Nf3 Nc6], defending the pawn. The Vienna [Nc3] covers d5 and keeps f4 in reserve. The engine cannot tell the two apart.

Quieter set-ups are about equal: [d3], [Ne2], [a3], [a4] and the Bishop's Opening [Bc4], which aims at f7 at once. [Be2], [Bd3] and [h3] are slower still. Opening the centre straight away gives Black the easier game: in the Centre Game [d4], after [d4 exd4 Qxd4 Nc6] the queen has to move again. The Portuguese [Bb5] attacks nothing yet.

Early queen moves cost about a third of a pawn: the Napoleon [Qf3] and the Wayward Queen [Qh5] both aim at f7, hoping for [Qh5 Nc6 Bc4], but Black has time to defend and to chase the queen. [Qe2] blocks White's own bishop. The pawn moves [c3], [c4], [h4], [b3] and [g3] do little, and the King's Gambit [f4] offers a pawn with [f4 exf4]: sharp, but about half a pawn worse for White against best defence.

The bad moves give Black something for free. [Na3] and [Nh3] put a knight on the rim. [f3] takes the knight's best square and loosens White's king. [Qg4] runs into [Qg4 Nf6], which develops with tempo on the queen. [b4] drops a pawn to [b4 Bxb4], and [g4] invites [g4 d5], after which the c8 bishop eyes the g4 pawn. The Bongcloud [Ke2] gives up castling for nothing, and [Ba6] just gives a bishop away to [Ba6 Nxa6].

The depths agree that [Nf3] and [Nc3] are the best two, but not by how much. [Nf3] looks like half a pawn for White at depth 8 (+0.52), +0.35 at depth 16 and +0.18 at depth 25, while [Nc3] hardly moves, +0.12 to +0.17 at every depth. a: Black has 20 possible replies. Four of them stand out, keeping White's edge to about a third of a pawn according to the engine. The classical [d5] stops 2.e4 for good and invites the Queen's Gambit with [d5 c4]. [Nf6] does the same job with a piece: it stops 2.e4 without committing a pawn, and leaves Black free to choose between the Indian defences, such as the King's Indian with [Nf6 c4 g6] or the Nimzo-Indian with [Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4].

The quiet [e6] and [c6] are just as good. Both prepare ...d5 while keeping options open: after [e6], White's [e6 e4] turns the game into a French Defence, and after [c6], [c6 e4] leads to a Caro-Kann, while [c6 c4] brings a Slav.

A second group is sound but more committal, at around two-thirds of a pawn for White. The Dutch [f5] grabs e4 with a pawn and aims for kingside play, at the cost of loosening Black's king, which the sharp Staunton Gambit [f5 e4] tries to exploit. [g6] and [d6] let White build a big centre and plan to undermine it later, often transposing into a King's Indian. The Old Benoni [c5] and the Mikenas [Nc6] attack d4 straight away, but White usually answers by gaining space with tempo: [c5 d5] or [Nc6 d5].

Flank moves give White a free hand in the centre. [b6] and [b5] prepare ...Bb7 to fight for e4 from a distance, for example [b6 e4 Bb7 Bd3]. [a6] is a waiting move preparing ...b5. [Na6] and [Nh6] put a knight on the rim, and [h6], [a5] and [h5] do nothing for the centre or development.

Three replies are simply bad. [f6] takes the best square from the g8 knight and weakens the e8–h5 diagonal to Black's king. The Englund Gambit [e5] gives away a pawn after [e5 dxe5], hoping for tricks such as [e5 dxe5 Nc6 Nf3 Qe7 Bf4 Qb4], which hits both the bishop and b2. Worst of all, the Borg Gambit [g5] just drops a pawn to [g5 Bxg5]: about two pawns for White.

The best replies are steady across depths: [Nf6], [d5] and [e6] stay between -0.18 and -0.35 from Black's side at depths 8, 16 and 25, and [c6] climbs from -0.49 at depth 8 to -0.29, level with [Nf6]. The move a shallow search overrates is the English [b6]: at depth 8 it looks almost as good as [Nf6] (-0.32), but it costs almost a pawn at depth 16 (-0.98) and depth 25 (-0.87).

White's pawn stands in the centre, and the queen and the f1 bishop have open lines. Black has 20 replies, and four of them keep White's edge to about a quarter or a third of a pawn. The engine's figures for them are too close to tell apart.

[e5] answers like for like: it claims its share of the centre and opens Black's own bishop and queen. The usual follow-up is [e5 Nf3 Nc6], where most of the classical openings begin. The Sicilian [c5] fights for d4 from the side and makes the game unbalanced from the first move. The French [e6] and the Caro-Kann [c6] are quieter: both prepare ...d5 to challenge e4 at once, as in [e6 d4 d5] or [c6 d4 d5].

A second group gives White a little more, around half a pawn to two-thirds. The Nimzowitsch [Nc6] develops but blocks the c-pawn. The Pirc [d6] and the Modern [g6] let White build a big centre and plan to hit it later. The St. George [a6] and the Carr [h6] are waiting moves. The Scandinavian [d5] attacks e4 straight away, but after [d5 exd5 Qxd5] the queen comes out early and White gains time on it with [d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3].

Then come moves that cost Black most of a pawn. Alekhine's Defence [Nf6] attacks e4 and invites White to chase the knight with [Nf6 e5 Nd5]. The Ware [a5] does little, and the Owen [b6] prepares ...Bb7 to press on e4 from a distance. [Nh6] and [Na6] put a knight on the rim, and [h5] does nothing at all: each is worth more than a pawn to White.

The worst replies weaken Black's position or give a pawn away. The Barnes [f6] takes the best square from the g8 knight and opens the e8–h5 diagonal to Black's king, and [f5] simply drops a pawn to [f5 exf5]. [b5] gives one to [b5 Bxb5]. The very worst is the Borg [g5]: after [g5 d4], the c1 bishop already attacks the g5 pawn, and White is close to two pawns up.

The shallow search gets this position badly wrong. At depth 8 the Scandinavian [d5] looks like Black's best reply by far, costing only six hundredths of a pawn, and the Sicilian [c5] and the Pirc [d6] come next; deeper, [d5] drops to -0.84 at depth 16 and -0.64 at depth 25, and [d6] to -0.56. [e5] and [c6] go the other way: about half a pawn worse than equal at depth 8 (-0.54 and -0.53 from Black's side), they are among the best four at depth 25 (-0.26 and -0.34). [b6] also looks better than it is at depth 8 (-0.51) and costs almost a pawn deeper.

White has 20 possible first moves: 16 pawn moves and 4 knight moves. The engine rates the best of them as practically equal, each worth about a third of a pawn to White. That small edge is simply the advantage of moving first.

The two classical moves put a pawn in the centre straight away. [e4] is the most popular: it takes the centre and opens lines for the queen and the f1 bishop, and usually leads to open, tactical games, such as [e4 e5] or the Sicilian [e4 c5]. [d4] does the same with the queen's pawn, which the queen already protects. Its games tend to be more strategic, and its main road is the Queen's Gambit, [d4 d5 c4].

The engine's favourite by a hair is [Nf3], the Réti, which fights for the centre with a piece and stops ...e5. Like the English [c4], it keeps every option open and often transposes into 1.d4 openings, as in [Nf3 d5 d4]. After [c4 e5], White is playing a Sicilian with colours reversed and an extra tempo. [g3] and [b3] prepare to bring a bishop out on a long diagonal.

Then come modest moves that keep the balance but give up most of White's edge. [e3] and [d3] open only one bishop's diagonal, [c3] takes the c3 square from the knight, and [Nc3] blocks the c-pawn. Flank moves such as [a3], [h3], [b4], [a4] and [h4] do even less for the centre. Bird's Opening [f4] controls e5 but loosens White's king, which From's Gambit [f4 e5] tries to exploit.

The worst first moves harm White's own position. [Na3] and [Nh3] put a knight on the rim, where it controls few squares. [f3] takes the best square from the g1 knight and opens the e1–h4 diagonal to White's king, which leads to the fastest checkmate in chess, Fool's Mate: [f3 e5 g4 Qh4]. The engine's very worst is the Grob [g4], which loosens White's kingside for nothing: after [g4 d5], the c8 bishop already eyes the g4 pawn.

How far the engine looks changes its favourite. At depth 8 [e4] is clearly the best first move, worth +0.53, and [Nf3] and [d4] are only +0.26 and +0.23; at depth 16 [e4] has come down to +0.35, and at depth 25 to +0.29, while [Nf3] has grown to +0.37 and [d4] to +0.31. The three end up too close to separate, so the shallow search's preference for [e4] is an artefact of depth, not a real edge.
